title: Goat Light Soup
author: Afua Boateng
desc: The tomatoes and onions are cooked, pulled out, blended and returned — which is what makes light soup light rather than a stew.
longDesc: Light soup is the broth that fufu is eaten with, and the technique that defines it is the removal and return: the tomatoes, onions and garden egg are cooked in the soup, lifted out, blended smooth, and stirred back in. Nothing is fried, so the soup stays thin and clean-tasting and red rather than orange. Five hundred grams of goat is marinated ten minutes in a blended paste of ginger, garlic, chilli, onion and tomato, cooked gently, given tomato puree and then half a litre of water, and simmered until the meat is tender.
ingredients: 500 g diced goat, or half a chicken, diced
1/2 kpakpo shito, or other hot pepper
steps: Blend the ginger, garlic, chilli, one onion and three of the tomatoes to a paste.
Marinate the meat in the paste for 10 minutes.
Cook the meat gently for 10 minutes.
Add the tomato puree and cook a further 10 minutes.
Add 500 ml of water and simmer until the meat is tender.
Add the remaining three tomatoes, diced, the diced aubergine and the last onion, and cook 30 minutes.
Remove the onions and tomatoes, blend them, and return them to the soup.
Bring back to a simmer, season, and serve with fufu (GHA001).
chefTips: Nothing is fried. That is the whole distinction between light soup and a Ghanaian stew, and it is why the soup reads as clean and thin.
Cook the vegetables, remove them, blend them, return them. The removal and return is the technique — blending them raw into the pot at the start gives you a different, duller soup.
Goat is the first choice and chicken the alternative, in that order, which matches how the dish is eaten in Ghana.
Kpakpo shito is the small round Ghanaian chilli and it is aromatic rather than merely hot. Half of one is the printed amount; a scotch bonnet is hotter and less fragrant.
Garden egg is the Ghanaian aubergine — small, pale and slightly bitter. It is cooked into the soup and blended back in, so it thickens very slightly while adding that bitter edge.
Until the meat is tender is the only cue for the long simmer, and goat can take well over an hour. Do not rush it to the thirty-minute vegetable stage.

Published figures for this soup vary enormously — one lab-standardised version uses 317 g of tomato and 15 g of salt per litre, another gives most amounts as 'a handful' or 'a small tin'. Use this one as the quantified household version.
commonMistakes: Frying the aromatics first, which makes it a stew.
Blending the vegetables in rather than cooking, removing and returning them.
Moving to the vegetable stage before the goat is tender.
Substituting scotch bonnet for kpakpo shito without expecting a different flavour.
Leaving out the garden egg, which carries the bitterness the soup is built on.
sources: Adapted from 'Traditional Ghanaian recipes • Goat light soup', Time Out Accra, 7 June 2013. BYLINE FLAG: NO AUTHOR is credited; the publication is cited, not an individual. No yield is printed. Quantities were confirmed across two fetches of the page (TWO-PASS).

Ingredients exactly as printed: 500g diced goat or half a chicken, diced; 6 whole tomatoes; Half a kpakpo shito (or hot pepper); 10g ginger; 10g garlic; 2 onions; 50g tomato puree; Salt; 1 aubergine (also known as a garden egg in Ghana); Fufu, banku or rice.

Method as printed: blend ginger, garlic, chilli, one onion and three tomatoes to a paste and marinate the meat '10 minutes'; cook the meat 'gently for 10 minutes'; add tomato puree for '10 minutes', then '500ml of water' and 'simmer until the meat is tender'; add the remaining three diced tomatoes, the diced aubergine and the last onion and cook '30 minutes'; remove the onions and tomatoes, blend and return, bring to a simmer and season.
PAGE TYPO, recorded: the method prints '10 minutesadd water' with the words run together. Read as 10 minutes, then add the water.
DONENESS CUES: only 'until the meat is tender'. The page gives NO sensory endpoint beyond that.

THE DISAGREEMENT ACROSS LIGHT SOUP SOURCES is wide and is not reconciled. A lab-standardised version — Appiah CA, Samwini AM, Brown PK, Hayford FEA, Asamoah-Boakye O, 'Proximate composition and serving sizes of selected composite Ghanaian soups', African Journal of Food, Agriculture, Nutrition & Development 20(3):15898-15918, 2020, affiliation KNUST, ingredients sampled at Ayigya market in Kumasi — gives per litre of boiling water: 5 g red chili powder, 15 g salt, 317 g tomatoes, 229 g onions, 354 g egg plant, plus 268 g broiler chicken thigh in its meat variant. Its method boils 'until the onions and tomatoes were soft', cooks the eggplant separately in 750 ml water for 20 minutes, blends it with 500 ml water and sieves it in, then boils 15 minutes. THAT IS A LAB-STANDARDISED RECIPE, NOT A CULINARY ONE, it names no ethnic origin, and it is recorded here for comparison rather than published as a recipe. Note its 15 g of salt per litre, which is far more than a household would use.

ANOTHER SOURCE, flagged for a byline conflict and not used for quantities: Chris Ndetei, 'How to prepare light soup with fish', yen.com.gh, 18 April 2018. The page byline reads 'Chris Ndetei' but Wikipedia's Light soup article attributes the same URL to 'Sasa, Tuandike'. THE BYLINES CONFLICT AND COULD NOT BE RESOLVED. Its amounts are mostly unquantified ('handful', 'small tin') in any case. It does carry one usable cue, quoted: 'Let the soup cook for a minimum of 20 minutes and a maximum of 25 minutes', with vegetables boiled until 'the skin peels'.

CONTEXT ONLY, no recipe: Catherine Forson Agbo, 'Appreciating Fufu and Light Soup, One Of Ghana's Dish', modernghana.com, 23 February 2019, places light soup with the Akan peoples of the Eastern and Ashanti regions and calls it 'the traditional complement' to fufu, listing ebunuebunu, groundnut and palm nut soups as the other fufu partners. That is the basis for the Akan community attribution above, since the recipe page itself names no community.
reheating: Simmer gently. It takes reheating better than most soups.
healthBenefits: No oil is added at any stage, which makes this one of the leanest West African soups.
Goat is lower in fat and cholesterol than beef or lamb.
High in lycopene from the long-cooked tomato.
Ginger and garlic both have documented anti-inflammatory activity.
culturalNote: Light soup is what a Ghanaian household makes when someone is unwell, and also what gets cooked on a Sunday with goat in it — a broth that stretches from convalescent food to celebration depending on what goes in the pot. Its name is literal: light, as against the heavy groundnut and palm nut soups that are the other things fufu is eaten with.
